title: What “five-star” means on the Nile
standfirst: Almost every Nile cruise ship calls itself five-star. The label tells you less than you might expect, and this page explains why and what to look at instead. It is part of our guide to [[up]].

sections.heading: Where the stars come from
paragraphs: Star ratings for Nile cruise ships are official classifications, but they were set for a different time and are rarely revisited. In practice, most ships on the river carry five stars, from tired older boats to the newest and most expensive.

sections.heading: Why the label covers such different ships
paragraphs: A rating checks that facilities exist: a restaurant, a pool, air conditioning. It does not measure how well they are kept, how many crew there are per guest, how large the cabins are or how good the food is. Those are the things that make two five-star ships feel completely different.

sections.heading: What to look at instead
paragraphs: Look at the cabin size in square metres, the number of guests, the crew per guest, the age of the last refit and independent reviews. Our own evaluation scores each vessel out of 100 against seven weighted criteria, from hygiene to service, so that two ships with the same stars can be told apart.

faqs.q: Is a five-star Nile cruise really five-star?
faqs.a: Sometimes. The label is common and broad, so judge each ship by its cabin size, crew, upkeep and reviews rather than by the stars.

faqs.q: Are there luxury ships above five-star?
faqs.a: Some ships describe themselves as five-star deluxe or luxury. Treat those as marketing terms and compare the facts.

seoTitle: What five-star means on a Nile cruise
seoDescription: Why almost every Nile cruise ship is five-star, and what to compare instead: cabins, crew, upkeep and independent evaluations.
